title: Can Stars Take It with Them?
text:
Wall Street firms compete fiercely to hire star equity analysts, the people who research companies and advise investors. Each year, the magazine Institutional Investor publishes a ranking of the best analysts, which gave Boris Groysberg, Linda-Eling Lee and Ashish Nanda of Harvard Business School a measure of performance over time.

They followed more than a thousand ranked star analysts from the late 1980s through the mid-1990s and compared those who changed firms with those who stayed. If talent were purely personal, the movers should have performed as well after switching as before.

They did not. On average, stars who moved to a new firm saw their rankings fall, and the drop lasted for years. The researchers concluded that much of a star's performance depended on the old firm's resources, colleagues, research support and reputation.

There were important exceptions. Analysts who moved to firms with stronger capabilities fared better. And analysts who moved together with their team, taking their junior colleagues and assistants with them, did not suffer the same decline. What made a star shine turned out to be partly the team around them.
lesson: When you hire a star, you are not buying their team, systems or reputation. Hire whole working groups when you can, or give newcomers time to rebuild theirs.
people: Boris Groysberg, Linda-Eling Lee, Ashish Nanda
location: Wall Street investment firms, New York, USA
source: Groysberg, B., Lee, L.-E., and Nanda, A. (2008). Can they take it with them? The portability of star knowledge workers' performance. Management Science, 54(7), 1213-1230.
